The Windows 11 media flyout is a transient XAML popup, not a child window of explorer.exe — that's why Process Explorer loses it as soon as the menu closes. Two options:

1. UI Automation: use `Desktop(backend="uia")`, trigger the flyout, then immediately enumerate top-level windows and grab the one whose class is `Windows.UI.Core.CoreWindow` or whose title/text mentions the playing track. You must catch it right after opening since it disappears on focus loss.
2. Skip the UI entirely: query the actual data source via the `GlobalSystemMediaTransportControlsSessionManager` WinRT API (through the `winsdk` or `winrt` Python packages). It gives you the current session's title/artist/play-state and lets you send transport commands (play/pause/next) directly — far more reliable than scraping a popup that only exists momentarily.

Missing info: which pywinauto backend/version you're currently using — if you're on the default `win32` backend, switching to `uia` alone may already reveal the window.

From the snippet, the most likely bug: you're hitting `logout.php`, not the actual login endpoint — a logout page will never contain "Invalid Login Details", so every attempt looks like a success. Separately, if the real login does redirect after POST, `requests` follows redirects by default, and the fail message is often only rendered via a session-tied flash message on the page immediately after a failed POST — without a persistent `requests.Session()`, each POST is a fresh anonymous client that may get a generic page missing the fail phrase entirely.

Fix: point the script at the real login URL, use `session = requests.Session()` and reuse it for every attempt, and sanity-check by printing `response.text` for one deliberately wrong password to confirm the exact fail phrase (case, punctuation) actually appears before trusting the `in` check:

```python
self.fail in response.text
```

ttk widgets don't carry a per-widget `font` option by default — appearance comes from the ttk style system, so `label['font']` is empty unless you set it explicitly. Get the font through the style instead:

```python
import tkinter.font as tkfont
from tkinter import ttk

style = ttk.Style()
style_name = label.cget("style") or "TLabel"
font_spec = style.lookup(style_name, "font") or "TkDefaultFont"

font = tkfont.nametofont(font_spec) if isinstance(font_spec, str) else tkfont.Font(font=font_spec)
for key, value in font.config().items():
    print(f"{key:>10}: {value!r}")
```

`style.lookup` walks the widget's assigned style name (default `"TLabel"`) through the active theme; if nothing overrides it, it resolves back to `TkDefaultFont`, matching plain `tkinter.Label`'s behavior.

Use `Series.where`, which replaces values failing the condition with NaN by default — it naturally handles blanks and existing NaNs too, since they're also not in your keep-list:

```python
df['name'] = df['name'].where(df['name'].isin(values_to_keep))
```

`.isin()` returns `False` for `''`, `np.nan`, and anything not in `values_to_keep`, so `.where()` masks all of those to NaN in a single pass — no separate handling of blanks/NaN needed.

This looks less like a model-accuracy problem and more like a digit-ordering problem: when you split the multi-digit image into individual glyphs (contours/connected components), the extraction order isn't guaranteed left-to-right — `cv2.findContours` returns them in whatever order the algorithm discovers, which is consistent with "1234" coming back as a scrambled "3356"-style result even though each single-digit crop looks fine and your model scores 96.9% on MNIST.

Fix: sort the extracted boxes by x-coordinate before predicting:

```python
boxes = [cv2.boundingRect(c) for c in contours]
boxes.sort(key=lambda b: b[0])
```

Then crop/predict in that order and concatenate the digit predictions. If results are still wrong (not just reordered) after sorting, check `padding_and_resize`/thresholding against MNIST's exact preprocessing (centering, stroke thickness, black-on-white vs white-on-black) — mismatches there degrade accuracy on real photos even when isolated single-digit MNIST accuracy is high.

Attach the parsed result to the field object inside the validator — validators receive the live `field` instance, and anything you set on it persists for the rest of the request:

```python
def data_validator(form, field):
    try:
        field.parsed_data = parse(field.data)
    except Exception as err:
        raise ValidationError(f"Invalid data: {err}") from None
```

Then after `form.validate_on_submit()` succeeds, just read it back instead of parsing again:

```python
if form.validate_on_submit():
    result = form.datafield.parsed_data
```

This works because validation always runs before you check the return value, so `parsed_data` is guaranteed present on success. Just don't rely on it existing when validation fails.

They produce the same result. `.filter(has=...)` is a method on an already-built `Locator`, while `has=` on `page.locator()` bakes the same filter into the initial selector — internally `locator(selector, **kwargs)` is sugar that forwards those kwargs into `.filter()`. There's no behavioral or performance difference; the choice is about composability: `.filter()` lets you narrow a locator you already have in hand (built elsewhere, reused, chained), while `has=` only works at the moment you write the selector. Prefer `.filter()` when refining an existing locator, and `has=` when writing the selector fresh in one line.

snscrape doesn't add its own geo-filtering — it forwards your query string verbatim to Twitter's search syntax, so location filtering uses the same `near:`/`within:` operators as twitter.com's advanced search, appended to the keyword string:

```python
keyword = '(COVID OR Corona Vírus) near:"São Paulo" within:15km'
```

This only works because the legacy search backend still parses `near:`/`within:`; it's not a dedicated snscrape parameter, so matches depend on Twitter's own geo-resolution of the place name (city names work more reliably than raw coordinates). For precise post-hoc filtering, check `tweet.coordinates`/`tweet.place` on returned objects instead, since not every matching tweet is geotagged. Missing info: whether you need only geotagged tweets or just ones mentioning/near a place name.

`pyqt6-tools` hasn't had a release since 2022, and its `sip`-based build backend doesn't support Python 3.12's packaging metadata handling — that deprecation warning escalating into a hard failure is the actual blocker, not something fixable via pip flags on 3.12.

Use Python 3.10 or 3.11 for this project instead:

```
py -3.11 -m venv venv
venv\Scripts\activate
pip install pyqt6-tools
```

If you only need Qt Designer and not the whole wrapper, install `PyQt6` plus a standalone Designer package (e.g. `pyqt6-plugins`/`qt6-applications`) or grab Qt Designer directly from the Qt installer — that avoids the broken `sip` build on newer Python entirely while still giving you the designer GUI.

They're not redundant. `case str():` does perform an `isinstance()` check under the hood, but `match`/`case` adds things a `type()`/`isinstance()` chain can't do cleanly: structural destructuring, guards, and OR-patterns in a single readable block:

```python
match point:
    case Point(x=0, y=0):
        print("origin")
    case Point(x=0, y=y):
        print(f"on y-axis at {y}")
    case [x, y] if x == y:
        print("diagonal")
```

For a plain "what type is this" check with no unpacking, `type()`/`isinstance()` stays simpler and more idiomatic — reach for `match` when you need to branch on *shape* (class fields, sequence/mapping contents) alongside type. One gotcha your example already handles correctly: `bool` is a subclass of `int`, so `case bool():` must come before `case int():`.

This isn't really solvable by tuning the trigger further — `GroupByKey`/triggers guarantee a pane fires per key per window, but panes for different windows of the same key can still be processed concurrently across bundles/workers. A non-atomic read-modify-write against a shared file inside a `DoFn` is inherently racy under that model.

Instead of trying to make windowing serialize this, make the state access itself sequential using the Stateful DoFn API, which Beam guarantees processes one element at a time per key:

```python
class MergeFn(beam.DoFn):
    BUFFER = beam.transforms.userstate.BagStateSpec('buf', beam.coders.StrUtf8Coder())
    def process(self, kv, buf=beam.DoFn.StateParam(BUFFER)):
        buf.add(kv[1])
```

Alternatively, write each firing to its own distinct output file and merge them in a separate, deterministic downstream step rather than mutating one shared file in place.

Reshape to long form first, then let seaborn group by the original column name via `hue`:

```python
import seaborn as sns

long_df = df.melt(var_name='Question', value_name='Answer')
sns.countplot(data=long_df, x='Answer', hue='Question')
```

`melt()` stacks Q1/Q2/Q3 into one `Answer` column plus a `Question` label column; `countplot` then draws grouped bars per unique answer value, colored by which question it came from, all on one axis. If you'd rather have one subplot per question instead of grouped bars on a shared axis, use `sns.catplot(data=long_df, x='Answer', col='Question', kind='count')` instead.

A `Combobox` only supports single selection by design, so filtering "by more than one value" needs a widget built for multi-select — swap it for a `Listbox` with `selectmode=MULTIPLE`, and change the filter logic from equality to set membership:

```python
self.filters_lb = Listbox(combofr, selectmode=MULTIPLE, exportselection=False)

def select_from_filters(self, event=None):
    selected = {self.filters_lb.get(i) for i in self.filters_lb.curselection()}
    for row in self.tree.get_children():
        values = self.tree.item(row)['values']
        visible = not selected or values[col_index] in selected
        # detach()/move() row based on `visible`
```

Keep using `tree.detach()`/`tree.move()` to hide/show rows instead of deleting them, so the original dataset survives across repeated filter changes.

The DOM itself isn't shown, so this can't be fully confirmed, but the classic cause of duplicated items alongside substring class selectors is that `div[class*='product-info']` matches on a partial class-attribute string, which can hit both an outer wrapper and a nested child that each happen to contain "product-info" — so one real product gets collected twice, taking different if/else branches depending on which matched node's price text is read.

Fix: use an exact class match instead of the substring selector, and dedupe by URL as a safety net regardless of cause:

```python
items = content.find_elements(By.CSS_SELECTOR, "div.product-info")
seen = set()
for it in items:
    url = it.find_element(By.CSS_SELECTOR, "a").get_attribute('href')
    if url in seen:
        continue
    seen.add(url)
```

This error means `INSTALLED_APPS` no longer evaluates to a `list`/`tuple` — almost always a typo introduced while adding the new entries, commonly either using `+=` with a bare string (`INSTALLED_APPS += 'corsheaders'`, which behaves oddly since strings are iterables of characters) or switching the brackets to `{ }` by accident while pasting.

Open `settings.py` and confirm it's still a plain list literal with commas between every entry, including the new ones:

```python
INSTALLED_APPS = [
    ...
    'corsheaders',
    'whitenoise.runserver_nostatic',
]
```

If appending programmatically, always add a list, not a raw string: `INSTALLED_APPS += ['corsheaders']`. Also check there isn't a second, later assignment to `INSTALLED_APPS` further down the file that overwrites the list with something else — that produces the exact same error.

The HTML form is malformed: `<form ... action='/', method=""post enctype="multipart/form-data">` has a stray comma after the action value and a broken `method=""post` attribute. Because of that, the browser doesn't parse `method="post"` and the form falls back to `GET` — GET can't carry file uploads, so `request.files` is empty server-side and `request.files['imagefile']` raises `BadRequestKeyError`.

Fix the tag:

```html
<form class="p-3 text-center" action="/" method="post" enctype="multipart/form-data">
```

Also guard the server side so a missing file fails clearly instead of throwing raw 400s:

```python
if 'imagefile' not in request.files:
    return "No file part", 400
imagefile = request.files['imagefile']
```

Two corrections to your reading:

- `\w` already includes `[A-Za-z0-9_]`, so `[\w_]` is redundant — the extra `_` adds nothing new, likely just defensive/careless writing by whoever wrote it.
- `[^_]` is a negated character class: the `^` inside `[...]` means "any character except", not "must be". So `[^_]$` means the last character must NOT be an underscore, the opposite of what you inferred.

Putting it together: the string must start with a letter, followed by 2–23 word/underscore characters, followed by one final character that is anything but an underscore — total length 4 to 25, and trailing underscores are forbidden (e.g. `foo_` fails, `foo_1` passes).
